title: Heavy rainfall and atmospheric conditions
text: Heavy rainfall can occur when moist air rises rapidly and condenses in deep clouds. Common supporting conditions include abundant atmospheric moisture, strong upward motion, low-pressure systems, active fronts, monsoon convergence, and thunderstorms. Orographic lifting can enhance rainfall near hills and mountains.

title: Thunderstorms and intense rain
text: Thunderstorms can produce intense short-duration rainfall, lightning, gusty winds, and sometimes hail. A thunderstorm weather code is not by itself an official government warning; official alerts should be verified against the relevant meteorological authority.

title: Indian monsoon rainfall
text: Indian monsoon rainfall is influenced by seasonal moisture transport, monsoon circulation, low-pressure systems, troughs, and local convection. Heavy rainfall episodes can be highly localized and can vary substantially between nearby districts.

title: Orographic rainfall
text: When moist air is forced upward over elevated terrain, it cools and condenses. This process can increase cloud development and rainfall on windward slopes and is called orographic lifting.

title: Low pressure and rainfall
text: Low-pressure systems can support convergence and rising air. When sufficient moisture is present, this can lead to widespread cloud formation and periods of moderate or heavy rainfall.

title: Rainfall probability interpretation
text: Precipitation probability describes the probability of measurable precipitation during the forecast period. It should not be interpreted as the percentage of a city that will receive rain or as a direct measure of rainfall intensity.

title: Rainfall amount versus probability
text: Rainfall amount and precipitation probability answer different questions. A high probability with a small rainfall amount can indicate likely light rain, while a lower probability with a large potential amount can indicate a less certain but potentially intense event.

title: Weather risk for outdoor activities
text: Outdoor activity decisions should consider precipitation probability, expected rainfall, thunderstorms, lightning, heat, wind, and official alerts. A general model recommendation is not a substitute for an official warning or local safety guidance.

title: Heat and humidity
text: High humidity can make hot conditions feel warmer because sweat evaporates less efficiently. Apparent temperature is useful for communicating heat stress, but activity decisions should also consider duration, hydration, shade, and individual health guidance.

title: Weather codes
text: Open-Meteo uses WMO weather interpretation codes. Examples include 0 for clear sky, 2 for partly cloudy, 3 for overcast, 61 for slight rain, 63 for moderate rain, 65 for heavy rain, and 95 for thunderstorm.

title: Current conditions versus forecasts
text: Current observations and future forecasts are different evidence types. Current temperature, cloud cover, wind, and weather condition should come from current observations. A future-day answer should use the forecast for the requested date rather than today's observation.

title: Official warning distinction
text: An application-level risk classification is not an official meteorological warning. Official warnings should be attributed only when the retrieved evidence explicitly identifies the issuing authority and warning level.

title: Flooding after intense rainfall
text: Flood risk after heavy rainfall depends on rainfall intensity and duration, drainage capacity, terrain, soil saturation, river conditions, and local infrastructure. Rainfall alone is not sufficient to determine whether a specific location will flood.

title: Forecast uncertainty
text: Weather forecasts have uncertainty that generally increases with forecast horizon and can vary by variable and location. Specific future-day claims should identify the forecast date and source rather than presenting forecasts as observations.
